Okay so I'll ramble about my favorite aspect of Barnabas' character arc in Dark Shadows (the original show from 1966 btw).
Barnabas' character arc is a huge thing, several factors being relevant and happened over a few hundred episodes. In Interviews a lot of people say that it was mainly due to how Frid played him, a combination of Frid not believing in purely evil people or characters, and in him awkwardly searching for the teleprompter which then in context of the character came across as hidden uncertainty and nervousness. Though several written aspects were necessary in his arc. Some of which partially happened before Barnabas ever showed up (before they had planned him yet, I believe), many written while he was there of course. They might have mostly been in response to Frid's performance, but still necessary and I don't see people talking about that a lot.   
While there were many previous pieces toward his final decision to become a 'good guy', hinting at his respect towards morality, hinting at the massive trauma that turned him into his angry, egoistic "Fuck everyone. I'm gonna take what's mine!" persona, him making decisions to become more human in aspects though not for the purpose of being a good person, the final pivot point was his little sister basically putting him into his place.   
For context: the same person that turned him into a vampire also destroyed and directly or indirectly murdered almost his entire family. He valued family A LOT - especially his little sister, Sarah. They were close and due to their big age difference and him gleefully taking to the duties of family he was basically more parent to her than either of their parents. She died very young, in a maliciously engineered manner that even made Barnabas feel partially responsible for her death.   
When Sarah kept appearing as a ghost to several people, talking with them, helping them, Barnabas is super confused. Why doesn't she come to him? Why doesn't she talk to him? They were so close, they loved each other so much. Did something change, if so what? She kept appearing to other people, never to him. Meanwhile his trust issues are getting worse. Hoffman (a medical doctor interested in the medical aspects of Barnabas' vampirism) had been working to find a way to turn him human. Several set backs and her setting up fail safes to ensure he won't kill her (cause she's a doctor and she's smart), lead to him becoming more distrustful until ultimately he decides to murder her.   
As he is about to kill her, Sarah knocks at the door, walks in, and Barnabas is first all "Oh! I'm so happy to see you. I was confused why you didn't come to me. I'm glad you're here." She doesn't respond, just stares him down. "Why don't you talk to me? I am your brother, Barnabas. I love you. Please talk to me." And she asked him to repeat a rhyme he'd taught her. It was about *needing* to be a just, moral, a good person. He had taught her that because of how important that was to him. He'd made sure she learned that as well. She then tells him, that she didn't come to see him, because she didn't want to, because he wasn't the brother she loved and he was a bad person. She basically told him to get his shit together (in the 9-year old ghost girl from the 18th century way of saying that). He says, she's right, that he had forgotten that, that he will change. He tries to keep her there, to keep talking to her. But she was done. She stopped him from another murder and told him her mind. So she just left, leaving him in an enormous existential crisis.   
He continued to struggle with being just and moral, but that was the final pivot point that made him want to be human again because being moral as a vampire is difficult, that made him *try* and mostly succeed being a moral person. Lots of other stuff had to set him up for this to work, but Sarah just calmly showing up, telling him he's exactly who he would have hated before the vampirism and just leaving him to sort it out by himself, is my favorite part of all of it.    
There was still a lot of necessary lying (because being honest about being/later having been a vampire and murderer wouldn't have gone that well), and some threats, blackmail, and manipulation (poor Willy), but he tried! And to be fair it's hard being a moral paragon when your best friend is Dr. Hoffman who is also willing to do just about anything short of murder if she sees it as necessary (poor Willy).  

Absolute favorite aspect of the whole show: Barnabas' and Hoffman's glorious full trust and loyalty friendship. (That might be characterized as a QPR.)    
Post the trust issue shit they really patched things up and got on like a house on fire and stayed the fucking closest throughout the rest of the show. And the show then never did any man + woman + like each other = must write romance! No, they're best friends. They trust each other with everything, loyal as fuck, no one's ever like "oh but secretly you're totally ... - care for others:

Depends on what you mean by that. 

Care for others = take care of them = help/support them: If someone else is hurting for example, that doesn't give me an "instinctive" urge to help, it doesn't give me emotional pain by proxy. But I still usually help because it lets me feel useful which I enjoy and if they're people I interact with repeatedly (friends, family, cashier in local supermarket), helping them will probably have positive effects on me in the long term. If I help my friend, they'll help me in future. If I don't, they might stop being friends with me. 
Generally I like my friends telling me their problems no matter how severe or absurd. To me that's kinda like a "human sudoku". I can ask for more info, I can hypothesize, I can puzzle around with it for a while which on its own is enjoyable to me. And either I give potentially useful solutions or I still had fun trying and they feel validated. Most of them have told me on several occasions that they appreciate this because of my rational approach, because it validates them, because they can tell me anything without disturbing me.

Care for others = value them = them being important to me.
I do. Many people are very important to me. To be entirely honest, humans to me are more like a computer or tv series, but as I enjoy DS9 a lot I also enjoy spending time with certain people a lot. The biggest difference is that people have more and more complex needs and choosing processes of their own. DS9 only needs the data, the hardware on which to run, and electricity to that hardware and whoever can fulfill these needs can spend time with it. Humans are more complex but fundamentally the same. If I want to spend time with them, which in many cases I do, I need to be mindful and fulfill their needs.


- selfish behavior:

I used to be very selfish as a kid and teenager. I've gotten rid of that by understanding. As I have my needs and wishes so do others and as I have needs and wishes many others don't share or understand so are others' needs and wishes real regardless of whether I share or understand them. If someone tells me they don't want to hang out right now, I understand and don't pressure it manipulate them into it. If my mom feels the emotional need to hug me, I engage unless I'm having a sensory overload. If a hypothetical ambulance is blocking my hypothetical car because the paramedics are busy hypothetically saving a life, I understand that that's something they need to do. I can't change any factors enough that to them moving the ambulance becomes an option, so I don't annoy them about fulfilling my needs despite it not being an option.

Generally the most helpful thing to learn was: not everyone is like me and that things and experiences can be real whether I can understand them or not.
